title: Sodic and Alkaline Soil Preparation: Gypsum, Leaching and Rice
metaTitle: Sodic and Alkaline Soil Preparation: Gypsum and Leaching
metaDescription: Sodic and alkaline soil preparation: how to spot a sodic field, why gypsum and leaching with good water work, and how deep tillage, mulch and rice help.
excerpt: Sodic and alkaline soil preparation starts with a diagnosis, because a hard crust and slow drainage do not always mean the same problem. A sodic soil holds too much sodium, which makes the clay fall apart, seal the surface and block water. This guide follows the FAO bulletin on salt affected soils and two university extension papers. It shows what to test, what to add and how to plan the field.

blocks.text: A warning first. Sodic soil needs a laboratory test before you spend money on an amendment. Ask the BSWM or your DA regional office where to have the pH and the salts tested. Then ask your municipal agriculturist what to do for your own soil.
How to recognize a sodic soil

The FAO Soils Bulletin 39 describes sodic soils this way. Too much sodium sits on the clay, and the soil loses its structure. It then disperses, which means the soil crumbs break apart. A dense, hard crust forms on top and keeps seedlings from coming up. Water soaks in slowly and the field stays wet for a long time.

Colorado State University Extension adds a sign you can see. A brownish black crust sometimes forms on the surface, because the soil organic matter disperses. White salt crust points to a saline soil instead.

blocks.caption: Laboratory limits used by extension services (saturated paste)

blocks.text: The FAO bulletin says a sodic soil has a saturated paste pH of 8.2 or more, and in extreme cases above 10.5. It treats an exchangeable sodium percentage of 15 as the usual limit. It also notes that a high pH does not harm the plant directly. Instead, it lowers the supply of calcium, magnesium and some other nutrients. For salty fields near the sea, read our [saline soil guide](/land-preparation/saline-soil-preparation).
Sodic and alkaline soil preparation step by step

items.title: Test first
items.text: Get the pH, the salt level and the sodium level from a laboratory. The FAO bulletin also describes a gypsum requirement test, which tells you how much gypsum the soil needs per 30 cm of depth.

items.title: Replace the sodium with calcium
items.text: According to the FAO bulletin, reclaiming a sodic soil means removing much of the exchangeable sodium and replacing it with calcium in the root zone. Gypsum is the usual amendment, because it supplies soluble calcium. The bulletin calls gypsum the most widely used amendment, because it is cheap and easy to get.

items.title: Mix the gypsum into the top layer
items.text: The FAO bulletin says gypsum is normally broadcast and then worked in by disking or plowing. It cites a trial where gypsum mixed into the top 15 cm worked better than gypsum left on the surface. It also says shallower mixing beats deeper mixing, which dilutes the gypsum.

items.title: Leach with good water
items.text: Fast results need the amendment followed by leaching, which means flushing water through the soil to carry the replaced sodium away. Use water with low salt. The bulletin notes that one irrigation before the amendment helps wash out soluble carbonates.

items.title: Add organic matter
items.text: Straw, farm manure and green manure help too, but slowly. The bulletin says decomposition and root action dissolve calcium already in the soil. Colorado State and Minnesota extension both list organic matter, cover crops and manure for sodic soils.

items.title: Open the hard layer where one exists
items.text: The FAO bulletin reports that deep plowing, up to 100 cm, helped soils with hardpans or dense clay subsoil in trials. It worked by mixing in calcareous or gypsiferous subsoil. Ask a technician before you try it, because it needs the right subsoil.

blocks.title: Drain after you fix the soil
blocks.text: Minnesota extension warns that installing drainage tile on sodic soil before remediating the sodicity gives less than ideal results. Fix the sodium first, then drain. Test both the salt and the sodium before you dig any canal.

Rice is a good fit for sodic land. For the field work itself, see our [rice land preparation guide](/land-preparation/rice-land-preparation). The FAO bulletin says its high tolerance comes from its ability to stand a layer of water through the season. Flooding also lowers the pH. In one cited study, the pH fell from 8.8 to 7 twelve weeks after flooding. The bulletin calls rice an ideal crop during reclamation. It says rice and dhaincha are tolerant, wheat is only moderately tolerant and legumes like lentil are sensitive.

The bulletin also reports that older rice seedlings tolerate sodicity better. It suggests transplanting seedlings 35 to 40 days old instead of the usual 30 days. Mulch helps as well. In one cited trial, rice husk mulch 3 to 8 cm thick pushed salts deeper. The next rice crop then yielded more. Do not leave the land fallow, because the bulletin says fallowing pulls salts back up. Keep it cropped.

The FAO bulletin says sodic soils are low in organic matter, so they are usually short of nitrogen. Poor aeration also wastes some of it, so let soil tests and a technician set the fertilizer rate. The same bulletin says acids or acid forming materials, such as sulphur, can also work. They act slowly, because they must first turn into sulphuric acid in the soil.

blocks.title: Put the reclamation plan on a calendar
blocks.text: Add the lot to anee.io and the [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar) dates the soil test, gypsum spreading, leaching, organic matter and planting back from your planting day. Ask Anee, the [AI technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician), to read your notes in Tagalog or English.
blocks.label: Start free

blocks.text: Trees and beds on sodic land

For trees, the FAO bulletin describes pits 90 cm deep and 90 cm wide, filled with soil amended with gypsum and manure. It also describes auger holes 15 cm wide and 150 cm deep. These were filled with original soil, 2 kg of gypsum and 7 to 8 kg of manure. In those trials the roots mostly bypassed the sodic layer. The bulletin also shows a bed and ridge method that stores rain water and grows trees on sodic soil. Compare it with our [fruit tree land preparation guide](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

items: Treating a high pH or a hard crust with no soil test.
Spreading gypsum and leaving the water out. The sodium needs water to leave.
Mixing gypsum deep, which dilutes it.
Leaving the land fallow between crops.
Planting wheat or beans first, when rice or another tolerant crop would do better.

blocks.text: Questions about sodic and alkaline soil

items.q: What is the difference between sodic and saline soil?
items.a: Saline soil has too much salt, often with a white crust, and a pH below 8.5. Sodic soil has too much sodium on the clay, a pH above 8.5, poor drainage and a hard crust, according to Colorado State University Extension.

items.q: What does gypsum do in sodic soil?
items.a: Gypsum supplies calcium that replaces sodium on the clay, and leaching then removes the sodium. The FAO bulletin does not describe gypsum as a pH lowering product. It calls it the most widely used amendment for sodic soils.

items.q: Can I plant rice on sodic soil?
items.a: Yes. The FAO bulletin calls rice an ideal crop during reclamation, because it tolerates sodium and the flooding lowers pH.
No. Minnesota extension says drain tile on sodic soil before remediation gives less than ideal results, so treat the sodium first.
